All students are taught the same essential knowledge and skills for their grade or course, whichever Fleming County classroom or school they attend. Teachers align instruction and assessments to those shared expectations. Students have enough time to learn, practice, and demonstrate the essential learning.
Families can count on consistent learning expectations across schools, and students have the time they need to meet them.

Fleming County Schools identifies Priority Standards from the Kentucky Academic Standards to focus instruction and assessment on essential learning. At the start of instruction on each Priority Standard, students explain in their own words what they are expected to learn and why it matters. They might connect the learning to something they already know, a problem they can solve, or something they will need to do next.
Students can see a purpose for today's work and understand where they might use what they are learning.
100% commitment. Record WHAT and WHY separately; count as met only when both are evident.

Studying examples makes what quality work looks like visible before students are expected to produce it themselves.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students deepen their understanding when they do the thinking, connect ideas across subjects, and apply what they know to real problems. We work with families, community members, and local employers to design challenges that matter to students and to Fleming County. Through these experiences, students build the knowledge, skills, and confidence to contribute to their community and compete globally.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students should have a real say in what they explore, how they approach their work, and how they show what they know. When students bring their interests, strengths, talents, cultural knowledge, and lived experiences to their work, they help shape what happens in the classroom and take greater ownership of their learning.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student deserves meaningful opportunities to show what they know and can do through writing, performances, projects, portfolios, and presentations. Above all, their work should provide clear evidence of grade-level and real-world readiness by showing how well they apply the knowledge and skills expected at their grade level to solve problems, make decisions, and communicate their thinking in authentic situations. Their work should also reflect who they are, what interests them, and what they aspire to do.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe students should receive feedback tied to clear expectations for mastery while they still have time to act on it. Students use Proficiency Scales to study examples, recognize what quality work looks like, and check their own work in progress. With timely feedback, they can see where they stand, decide what to improve, and take ownership of their next step.
Support to Take the Next Step

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student deserves access to challenging grade-level learning and just-in-time support when they need it. Effective support helps students work through difficulty, do the thinking themselves, and take their next step with greater independence.

In Fleming County Schools, we believe every student can grow from where they are, master important knowledge and skills, build readiness for the next grade and life beyond school, and develop the agency to shape their own learning and future. Thriving also means feeling a sense of belonging, knowing yourself, developing socially and emotionally, and building habits that support physical health.

Students apply grade-level knowledge and skills to a real-world problem. They consider possible responses, use evidence to justify a solution or recommendation, and explain how the evidence shaped their decision. In a BRIDGE Performance Assessment, for example, students might compare options and defend a recommendation for a local challenge.
Students learn to weigh evidence and make decisions they can explain when they face a real problem.

Learning in Context and Across Subjects

When a real-world problem calls for more than one subject, students bring knowledge and skills from those subjects together. They explain what each subject helped them understand or do. For example, students might use science to explain a local issue, math to compare possible responses, and writing to communicate a recommendation.
Students see how learning from different classes works together when they face a problem outside the classroom.

Students produce multiple pieces of evidence that show what they know and how they can use it. Evidence from more than one piece of work gives students, families, and teachers a clearer picture of what students can do with their learning.

Proficiency Scales: Check Work in Progress

At least once during instruction on each Priority Standard with an aligned Proficiency Scale, students use the scale to check their own work in progress. They point to where the work meets the expectations and identify a specific next step while they still have time to act on it.
Students learn to spot what their own work needs while they can still improve it.

Students are introduced to the aligned Proficiency Scale for each Priority Standard and use it throughout learning to understand mastery expectations, gauge their progress, and identify next steps. They use the scale to analyze examples and check their own work as they develop and demonstrate mastery.

Students tackle real challenges that families, community members, or local workforce partners helped design. Partners might help frame the question, contribute information that shapes the task, or identify what a workable solution needs to accomplish. Students can point to how that contribution shaped the challenge they are working on.
Partners help students understand who faces the problem, what is at stake, and what a workable response would look like.

Students receive specific feedback tied to the Priority Standard or its Proficiency Scale while they still have time to use it. The feedback points to something in their work and helps them see where they stand. Students can explain what to keep doing or what to improve next.
Timely, specific feedback helps students know where to focus their effort before the work is finished.

Students act on feedback to improve their understanding or performance. They show what changed in an explanation, solution, draft, or performance and explain how the change better meets the learning expectation.
Students see how a specific change can strengthen their reasoning, correct a misunderstanding, or improve their performance.
